problems.description: Over-engineering: commit splits the single-file seed into repositories.py, notifications.py, and celery_config.py, adding Celery/notifications infrastructure to a tier-1 minimal todo API — speculative surface beyond the codebase scope and a churn risk for future story sessions.
init_db() now runs at module import time, creating an implicit side effect that couples DB schema creation to importability instead of an explicit startup path.

9 PEP8 convention violations introduced in new files (module-level constants not UPPER_CASE in celery_config.py/notifications.py/repositories.py, snake_case/PascalCase issues) driving measured convention score to 0.67.
Cognitive complexity +9 from the expanded validation branching in edit_task/add_task; the input guards could be factored into shared validators.
Discrepancy: 'Classes should use PascalCase' violations reported for app.py/test_app.py contradict the AST measurement of +0 classes added, so those specific flags look like checker false positives.

strengths: Removes dead/legacy code (_legacy_format_date, _notify_admin, fetch_task) — SonarQube smells delta −2
Fixes latent status bug where the seed inserted 'done' but returned 'pending'; inserts now default to 'pending' consistently
Timezone-aware datetime.now(timezone.utc) replaces deprecated datetime.utcnow()
Adds isolated pytest coverage using a tmp_path/monkeypatch DB fixture
Adds input validation and a consistent error() helper returning 400/404 JSON responses
Adds type hints and fetch-after-write so create_task returns the canonical row via get_task
commit_reviews.summary: Net improvement that removes dead code, fixes the status and timezone bugs, and adds tests and validation, but over-engineers the tier-1 app with Celery/notifications/repository modules and introduces 9 convention violations plus import-time init_db.

problems.description: Hand-rolled JWT built from raw hmac/base64 instead of an established library (PyJWT/jose); bespoke crypto implementations are an anti-pattern and a guaranteed rework target for the core auth deliverable.
Migration adds owner_id=NULL to existing tasks and silently hides them from all users ('not exposed'), making all pre-existing task data inaccessible after the auth feature ships.
No tests added for register/login/token-verification flows or owner-scoped queries despite +20 new functions; auth is security-sensitive and should be covered.

Cognitive complexity +18; token helpers, decorator, and auth routes are embedded inline in app.py instead of a dedicated auth module, even though the codebase already separates repositories.py/notifications.py/celery_config.py.

Measured convention score 0.67 with 9 violations, but most (celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py, test_app.py) are in files outside this commit's diff and pre-existing; only app.py is in-diff, so the commit's own code is largely convention-clean.

strengths: Password storage uses werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash rather than plaintext or custom hashing.
Constant-time hmac.compare_digest is used for signature verification.
All task queries are scoped by owner_id, giving correct per-user data isolation.
init_db upgrades existing schemas in place via PRAGMA table_info + ALTER TABLE without data loss.
New code follows existing module conventions (get_db, error helper, snake_case functions).
commit_reviews.summary: Coherent auth+ownership feature with correct query scoping and a safe in-place migration, but the hand-rolled JWT, silently orphaned legacy tasks, and zero new tests make it a net-negative commit.

problems.description: edit_task performs two lookups for the same row (previous_task via get_task, then update_task re-fetches); the notification transition check could reuse a single read without the duplicate 'task is None' guard.

The notification side effect is queued after the DB write is committed but before the response is sent; if the broker is unavailable, send_notification_email.delay raises and the client sees a 500 despite the state change already persisting.
No tests cover the new email validation branch or the email persistence/retrieval path; tests only exercise the username fallback behavior implicitly.

Several flagged violations (broker_url, result_backend, celery_app lowercase at module level) are false positives: Celery's config_from_object requires these exact lowercase attribute names, so the UPPER_CASE/UPPER_SNAKE convention checker misfires here.

strengths: Notification is queued only on a status transition to 'completed', preventing duplicate emails on repeated completion — verified by an explicit test.
Follows the established migration pattern (PRAGMA table_info check + ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN) for the new users.email column.
Clean async boundary: Celery task is isolated in its own module with routed config, keeping app.py focused.
Sensible fallback design — COALESCE(email, username) avoids null recipients in the mock email path.
Solid test coverage for the notification behavior using correct patch target (app.send_notification_email.delay).
commit_reviews.summary: A well-integrated, pattern-respecting feature (async email notifications with transition-only triggering and good tests), held back only by minor redundancy, non-atomic side effects, and mostly false-positive convention lint flags from Celery's required lowercase config names.

problems.description: BaseRepository.create/update interpolate column names into SQL via f-strings (values are parameterized, so no injection risk, but callers passing arbitrary keys could generate malformed SQL or touch unowned rows).
Generic BaseRepository.get_all/get_by_id are unscoped by ownership; future callers could bypass the owner_id guards the commit correctly preserved in the specialized methods.

New module repositories.py is lowercase, matching sibling modules but violating standard package naming; the flagged 'module-level constants UPPER_CASE' item for repositories.py is a false positive (ConnectionFactory is a type alias, not a constant).

7 of 9 measured violations (celery_config.py, notifications.py, test_app.py, app.py classes) pre-exist this commit and are untouched by it; convention score 0.67 reflects repo-wide state, not the new code, which is itself compliant.

strengths: Clean extraction of all raw SQL from the Flask view layer into TaskRepository/UserRepository, dramatically reducing app.py surface (AST +3 classes, -79 lines in app.py).

Repository pattern respects existing codebase structure: reuses the get_db connection factory via constructor injection, keeps owner_id scoping on every task query, and preserves the ALTER TABLE migration logic inside initialize().
Behavior-preserving refactor: ownership checks, 409/401 error paths, and update-by-owner semantics are all retained, just relocated.
The refactor reduces cognitive load on the view layer; +3 cognitive complexity is the repository layer absorbing branching that previously lived inline.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-executed, behavior-preserving extraction of persistence into a repository layer that fits the existing get_db/Flask architecture, though the generic unscoped base-class methods and dynamic column interpolation deserve guardrails.

problems.description: flask-limiter defaults to RATE_LIMIT_REDIS_URL=redis://localhost:6379/2, adding a hard runtime dependency on Redis to an app that previously only needed SQLite; a deploy without Redis (or without the env var) fails on the first rate-limited request. Tests mask this by monkeypatching MemoryStorage.

Pagination silently changes list ordering from ORDER BY created_at DESC to ORDER BY id DESC. Semantics happen to coincide (newer id == newer created_at) but the repository no longer honors the original ordering contract; should either keep created_at ordering with an id tiebreaker or document the change.
next_cursor is computed as tasks[-1]['id'] whenever len(tasks) == limit, so a full final page returns a cursor that yields an empty next page rather than None (off-by-one in page-awareness).

rate_limit_key decodes/verifies the JWT on every request to key the limit by user; reasonable, but it couples the rate limiter to token parsing and adds per-request overhead even for unauthenticated endpoints.

The 0.67 convention score reflects 9 pre-existing violations in files untouched by this diff (celery_config.py, notifications.py, plus pre-existing PascalCase/constant issues). This commit's own code introduces zero new violations, so the low score is not attributable to the diff.

strengths: Layered pattern preserved end-to-end: route -> service function -> repository, with pagination pushed down into TaskRepository.list_page_for_owner as efficient keyset queries.
Comprehensive tests: parametrized invalid-input coverage, two-page cursor walk, and a rate-limit test asserting 429 with Retry-After header.
Rate limit keyed by verified bearer-token user with IP fallback, avoiding shared-IP false positives.
Explicit input validation with clear 400 errors for cursor/limit, and env-configurable settings consistent with existing DATABASE/JWT_SECRET style.
commit_reviews.summary: Clean, well-tested addition of cursor pagination and rate limiting that respects the existing layered architecture, but it introduces a Redis runtime dependency, a subtle created_at->id ordering change, and inherits a 0.67 convention score driven by pre-existing violations in files this commit never touched.

compounding_issues: The 'legacy' compatibility user + data migration introduced in Session 2 (to preserve pre-auth tasks) remained permanently baked into repositories.initialize_database() through Sessions 4-5, keeping awkward migration logic in the codebase long after the auth transition was complete.

The single-file seed forced app.py to balloon to ~265 lines by Session 3 (auth + ownership + notification trigger), which is what created the need for Session 4's refactor; the bloat was repaid but only after it accumulated.

Repository layer (Session 4) instantiates a fresh TaskRepository(DATABASE)/UserRepository(DATABASE) object on every call and builds dynamic column SQL via f-strings in the base CRUD, a pattern that persisted into Session 5's pagination code.
Session 5's rate_limit_key() re-decodes the JWT on every request even though require_auth already decoded it — a minor redundant-work pattern that landed in the final commit.
key_decisions: Session 2: JWT auth with per-owner task isolation plus a legacy-user migration to keep pre-auth tasks accessible instead of dropping them.
Session 3: Celery async notification dispatch on a dedicated 'notifications' queue, with email sending mocked and dispatch gated on a pending->completed transition only (no duplicate sends).
Session 4: Repository pattern extraction — BaseRepository ABC + Task/User repositories moved all SQL out of app.py, leaving thin routes/models and enabling clean layering.
Session 5: Auth-aware rate limiting (Flask-Limiter keyed by authenticated user ID, IP fallback, in-memory fallback) and cursor-based pagination with strict limit/cursor validation.
Session 1: Import-time init_db() (rather than only under __main__) made the app WSGI/test-runner safe and established the testable-app foundation every later session built on.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across all five sessions. Session 1 hardened the seed (payload type validation, timezone-aware timestamps, import-safe DB init) and added the first 3 passing tests; Session 2 layered JWT auth and ownership with a thoughtful data migration; Session 3 integrated Celery for async notifications and showed good debugging when a failing test turned out to be a test bug (unregistered email) rather than a code bug. Session 4 was a behavior-preserving refactor — test count held steady at 6 while 126 lines of SQL left app.py into a clean repository layer — and Session 5 delivered the strongest technical work, adding cross-cutting rate limiting keyed per authenticated user and cursor pagination with edge-case validation, expanding the suite to 9 green tests and building naturally on the repository seam created in Session 4.
story_review.summary: A textbook progression — harden, feature, integrate, refactor, cross-cutting — where each session's architecture anticipated the next, culminating in a clean layered Flask API (routes + repositories + Celery tasks) with monotonically growing, always-green test coverage.
